Dynamic diagram (deployment view): Token-based API authorization.
Requirement: Authenticate users and authorize each API request.

A User [Person] signs in through a Web sign-in page [Container: Web app] with a username and password. Both the User and Web sign-in page are outside AWS Cloud. The page collects and submits the credentials to Amazon Cognito user pool over HTTPS; the page does not verify the password. Cognito verifies the password, authenticates the user and issues tokens. The ID token carries user attributes, for example cognito:username = alex; custom:tenantId = T-001; custom:type = Customer; cognito:groups = [Customers].

AWS Cloud [Deployment node] encloses Amazon Cognito user pool [Container: Amazon Cognito], Amazon Verified Permissions [Container: AWS managed service], Backend APIs [Container: REST API], and API enforcement [Software system boundary]. API enforcement encloses only Amazon API Gateway [Container: AWS managed service] and Lambda authorizer [Container: AWS Lambda]. API Gateway enforces the authorization result; Lambda authorizer verifies the token and queries policy; Amazon Verified Permissions makes policy decisions.

The Web sign-in page sends the token with each API request to Amazon API Gateway over HTTPS. API Gateway passes the token to the Lambda authorizer using a generic AWS invocation. The authorizer verifies the token and asks the Amazon Verified Permissions decision endpoint over HTTPS whether the request is allowed. If allowed, API Gateway forwards the request to Backend APIs over HTTPS. If authorization fails, API Gateway returns HTTP 403 with an authorization error message to the Web sign-in page over HTTPS.

Represent the main sequence as 1. Authenticate (returns tokens); 2. API request with token; 3. Pass token for authorization; 4. Query policy; 5. Forward allowed request. A separate bold 5' relationship represents the HTTP 403 failure response. Policy query is auxiliary and dashed; main calls are solid. Arrows point from caller to callee; return tokens are folded into the authentication label, rather than a second return arrow. User uses the Web sign-in page. Show the token example in a local comment near Step 1 and explain the notation in a legend. All calls remain inside shared enclosing domains and cross only required boundaries.

2.description:
The diagram is titled “Dynamic diagram (deployment view): Token-based API authorization.” Its requirement is to authenticate users and authorize each API request.

The architecture contains a User, typed as a Person, and a Web sign-in page, typed as a Container implemented as a Web app. Both are outside the AWS Cloud deployment node. The Web sign-in page collects and submits credentials; it does not verify the password.

The AWS Cloud deployment node contains an Amazon Cognito user pool, Backend APIs, Amazon Verified Permissions, and an API enforcement software system boundary. The API enforcement boundary contains Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda authorizer. Cognito, Backend APIs, and Amazon Verified Permissions are inside AWS Cloud but outside the API enforcement boundary. One element of each of these kinds is depicted; no instance multiplicities are specified.

The Amazon Cognito user pool is a Container using Amazon Cognito. It verifies the password, authenticates the user, and issues tokens. Amazon API Gateway is a Container using an AWS managed service and enforces the authorization result. The Lambda authorizer is a Container using AWS Lambda; it verifies the token and queries policy. Amazon Verified Permissions is a Container using an AWS managed service; it is the decision endpoint and makes policy decisions. Backend APIs is a Container implemented as a REST API.

The directed interaction sequence is:

0. The User uses the Web sign-in page, providing username and password. The arrow runs from the User to the Web sign-in page. No protocol is stated for this step.

1. The Web sign-in page calls the Amazon Cognito user pool to authenticate using username and password over HTTPS. This call crosses into AWS Cloud and is labeled “Authenticate (returns tokens).” The normal token return is folded into this step rather than drawn as a separate return arrow.

2. The Web sign-in page sends an API request with a token to Amazon API Gateway over HTTPS, on each request. This crosses into AWS Cloud and into the API enforcement boundary.

3. Amazon API Gateway passes the token to the Lambda authorizer for authorization. This is labeled a “Generic AWS invocation” and stays within the API enforcement boundary.

4. The Lambda authorizer queries Amazon Verified Permissions with “Query policy: is request allowed?” over HTTPS. This is a dashed arrow denoting an auxiliary policy query. It crosses out of the API enforcement boundary while remaining inside AWS Cloud.

5. If allowed, Amazon API Gateway forwards the allowed request to Backend APIs over HTTPS. This crosses out of the API enforcement boundary while remaining inside AWS Cloud.

5′. As the alternative failure response, if authorization fails, Amazon API Gateway sends HTTP 403 plus an authorization error message to the Web sign-in page over HTTPS. This crosses out of both the API enforcement boundary and AWS Cloud. The diagram does not specify the error message text.

An ID token example associated with Step 1 lists these attributes exactly:
cognito:username = alex
custom:tenantId = T-001
custom:type = Customer
cognito:groups = [Customers]

The legend identifies “[Type: technology]” as the C4 element caption and says outlined groups represent architectural domains. It defines 1–5 as the request sequence, with 5′ as the alternative failure response. A solid filled arrow means caller to callee; a dashed arrow means an auxiliary policy query. The yellow note supplies example ID token attributes. No separate return from the policy decision service or the authorizer, no token-verification method, and no policy rules are specified.

facts.claim: The main sequence is authenticate, API request with token, pass token for authorization, query policy, then forward the allowed request.
facts.evidence:
1. The Web sign-in page calls the Amazon Cognito user pool to authenticate with username and password over HTTPS. This interaction crosses into AWS Cloud. It returns tokens; the normal token return is folded into Step 1 rather than shown as a separate return arrow.

2. The Web sign-in page sends an API request with token to Amazon API Gateway over HTTPS, on each request. This interaction enters both AWS Cloud and the API enforcement boundary.

3. Amazon API Gateway passes the token to the Lambda authorizer for authorization, through a “Generic AWS invocation.” Both endpoints are inside the API enforcement boundary.

4. The Lambda authorizer queries Amazon Verified Permissions: “is request allowed?” This uses HTTPS and crosses out of the API enforcement boundary while remaining inside AWS Cloud. The query is drawn as a dashed arrow, denoting an auxiliary policy query.

5. If allowed, Amazon API Gateway forwards the allowed request to Backend APIs over HTTPS.
